components.text: Contacts the causal premise by offering apparently causeless differences between otherwise indistinguishable radioactive atoms.
Does not separately defeat the contingency-to-personal-explanation bridge for the universe as a whole.
The causal premise behind the inference from a finite beginning to a transcendent cause.
Contacts the grounding demand by asking what about God makes imposed norms morally right.
Mentions alternative ethical theories but does not explain how any one grounds objective values and duties.
The inference that divine commands or God uniquely ground objective moral rightness.
Contacts testimonial discrimination by comparing Christian miracle reports with other religious claims the audience would reject.
Does not directly assess the empty tomb, appearances, transformed belief, or their source independence.
Whether testimonial evidence discriminates resurrection from unreliable or analogous religious miracle claims.
Identifies the missing necessity premise: the argument must exclude every possible morally sufficient divine reason.
Does not itself identify and substantiate a particular morally sufficient reason for the actual pattern of suffering.
The unargued premise that no possible morally sufficient reason could justify divine permission of suffering.
Challenges Rosenberg's broader naturalistic framework by arguing that denial of persons and first-person perspectives conflicts with certain experience.
Does not answer the Euthyphro grounding dilemma or defend objective morality's dependence on God.
The availability of non-divine ethical theories and the grounding challenge to divine morality.
Identifies that virtual particles arise from a physical quantum vacuum rather than from nothing.
Challenges the assertion of causelessness by noting that deterministic interpretations of quantum mechanics remain available.
The claim that quantum events constitute uncaused beginnings relevantly analogous to cosmic emergence from nothing.
Identifies that disputing Rosenberg's additional philosophical doctrines does not logically refute atheism.
Does not provide a positive naturalistic account of intentional mental states or aboutness.
The inference from rejecting Rosenberg’s philosophical doctrines to rejecting atheism itself.
Contacts logical incompatibility by arguing that creaturely freedom constrains which good worlds are feasible for God.
Challenges the claim that an equally good world with less evil was feasible by placing the proof burden on that modal assertion.
Whether an omnipotent good God could have morally sufficient reasons tied to freedom and feasible worlds.
Contacts the cosmic distinction by relying on radioactive decay and symmetry breaking rather than only virtual particles from a vacuum.
Extends the quantum analogy directly to the assumption that the universe's earliest state requires a cause.
The distinction between quantum events in a physical vacuum and an absolute cosmic beginning requiring a cause.
The assumption that the universe’s earliest state must have a sufficient cause.
Contacts the feasibility claim by proposing free agents who always choose rightly or are not exposed to destructive temptation.
Challenges freedom as a morally sufficient reason for catastrophic suffering but does not exclude every possible sufficient reason.
Whether significant freedom requires agents ever to choose catastrophic wrongdoing or face suffering-producing temptation.
Whether freedom supplies a possible morally sufficient reason for the observed suffering.
Contacts the design inference by arguing that God adds no predictive contribution warranting scientific explanatory acceptance.
Extends the no-prediction criticism to divine explanation generally without separately analyzing cosmological explanatory content.
Whether design has evidential explanatory content sufficient to warrant preferring it over natural alternatives.
Contacts the claimed explanatory gap by offering natural selection as an account of shared cooperative moral norms.
Does not explain objective normativity or show why evolved dispositions are genuinely morally right.
Provides a positive naturalistic account in one domain but does not address intentionality or persons.
Whether objective moral normativity, rather than common cooperative behavior, has a non-divine ground.
Whether naturalism can explain human moral practices without theism.
Contacts arbitrariness by grounding goodness in God's essential character rather than unconstrained divine will.
Explains duties as commands reflecting that character, but does not independently justify identifying God's nature with goodness.
Does not contest the evolutionary account of cooperative dispositions or distinguish it empirically.
What non-arbitrarily makes God’s commands morally right.
Whether evolutionary origins of cooperation replace an account of objective moral grounding.
Identifies that predictability is not a necessary test when empirically equivalent theories differ.
Supplies simplicity, plausibility, ad hocness, and explanatory power as additional standards.
The premise that predictive contribution is the exclusive legitimate test of a hypothesis.
Whether theism can be assessed by broader explanatory standards even if disputed doctrines do not follow from atheism.
Contacts the self-refutation challenge by explaining communication as causal transmission that reorganizes neural circuits.
Addresses the apparent inconsistency of publishing claims while denying intrinsic statement content.
Does not bear on explanatory virtues or predictive standards.
The claim that denying intrinsic meaning or intentionality makes naturalistic communication self-refuting.
The claimed evident aboutness of thought as a reductio of materialism.
